While I want all of the special bells and whistles that they are implementing. Does anyone else think that it's entirely possible that they are making the game too realistic for the FPS community. I don't think that it's necessary for the FPS community to like the game in order for SC to be successful - but it would go a long way.

What do you guys think?
Do you guys think that the FPS community will accept SC?

I think it will appeal to many that like the games that go for realism like ARMA but those that prefer Call of Duty, Battlefield etc. where you can jump, run and change direction on a dime will be disappointed.

I prefer the direction they are going though, I think it will suit Star Citizen better since it's going for realism, if it was arcade-like it'd really feel out of place to me.

Honestly, I don't really care. FPS is a very broad genre. My hope is that gamers that like Battlefield and CoD will stay far away and that people that like more tactical combat from games like the old Rainbow Six and SWAT games will come over. After all, slow tactical FPSs are far and few between these days. Moreover, I think it also speaks to the older pc demographic that SC focused on. A slow highly tactical team-based FPS will also suit the game much better. Death of a spaceman and all of that. I really hope that it will be more like the old Rainbow Six games and less like Battlefield.

Personally I'd much rather see it lean more towards the realistic end. I'd hate to see it so vanilla that it invites the CoD crowd over. As Ross said, if it did feel more arcadey it wouldn't really line up with the rest of the vision for the game.

On another note, I sure hope they expand the MP maps before years end or else people grow really tired of FPS after a few short months. I'm in no way looking forward to the SATA ball stuff, so that leaves me with only the Gold Horizon map. Still can't wait to play it though.

I think that over all the FPS community will be interested in it, but there won't be a huge move from ArmA, CoD, or Battlefield and the like simply because those communities have been around over a decade. However this might really help draw attention to the game as a whole seeing as its a rather unique on the sim shooter. What will be the deciding factor are the FPS streamers and youtubers who are really the main force behind hype and popularity of the smaller and less known shooter titles, of which this is. However if you are referring to the FPS community in terms of twitch shooter titles like CoD and Halo (and to a lesser extent Battlefeild and Counter Strike) then no, those communities will not accept the game as it will be slow paced and probably a bit too brutal for them.

What I have seen so far looks great and I play almost FPS games exclusively. My current lineup is CS:GO, Halo: MCC, Insurgency, BF3/4, and L4D. I don't think they really need to be super innovative with it. They just need to stick to a core formula that works. Balanced weapons, good hit registration, and smooth player mechanics.

I think the most important issue for the FPS community is how the implement the "Star Marine" mini game to the PU. If I want to play a FPS match for a quick 30 mins- 1 hour I dont want to have to fly around for 20 minutes first. If they keep it like arena commander so you can get in and out rather quickly then I think it will fit in nicely.

I want to know if everything will be balanced the same in Star Marine as it is in the PU. If they dont balance it correctly we could end up with something similar to "Missile Commander" which would not be fun out all. Good thing its still in alpha.

I know people that are eagerly awaiting the FPS portion of things. I am also looking forward to the increased realism aspect of the SC FPS. I have a funny feeling that I am gonna end up being the courier since I am the only one in my small org that has a ship that can hold more than 2 people.

[WP] It's been one year since the outernet was established.

I could feel it pulsing. The thoughts of everyone on the bus pressed against each other competing for space. Everyone's mental bubble, so fragile like one, radiated and reflected the colours of their emotions. This was the Outernet. One year ago, today, everyone woke up the exact same way: confused, disoriented, and most important of all, with a killer headache. Doctors didn't what it was, but could inexplicably tell exactly what kind of pain their patients were experiencing. People couldn't lie all too well, everyone was able to tell instantaneously. Plenty of people were fired from their jobs because their bosses "had a feeling they were thinking rude thoughts." That's at will employment for ya.

Then there those like me. The Routers. Among the 10% of the world's population that could acutely perceive this new connection between people, it was more of a curse than a blessing a year ago. When two people interact, their mental bubbles stick to each other, exchanging a nexus of information so quickly that if you weren't ready for it, it could knock you on your arse. You'd suddenly knew way too much about a person way too quickly. Some went mad; forgetting who they were. I was lucky enough to be out on vacation, secluded from the world until I could at least block out the intrusive minds of the masses. It was kind of like us routers were plugged into whatever fourth dimensional shit turned on the Outernet, and everyone else used our connection wirelessly to do their own thing. We were the gate to that world.

Now that the Outernet is on, there is no longer an "off." You didn't dream up your own thoughts at night. If you were poor you suffered through the amalgamation of everyone else around you's thoughts every night. If you were rich, you curled into your faraday cage and had your personal Router play you a digital dream. You couldn't walk down a busy street without seeing an advertisement from a company's hired Router. Man, it's boring being corporate Router. I should know, I was one. Luckily, I moved away from the commercialized, legal side of the new and booming business.

Then there's me. The other side of that coin. I'm what they call a Virus, a Router who's strong enough to envelop other people's bubbles in my own, allowing me to analyze their thoughts in real time and had various amounts of control over their thoughts. There aren't many of us, for obvious reasons. Those who couldn't hide their talent we're either killed by those who were threatened by their power, or became the ones hunting other Viruses. Survival of the fittest and such. I'm more of a man of opportunity.

So that's what brings us here, on this packed bus in rural China passing by miles and miles of rice fields sitting too close to too many people. The opportunity in question, a man sitting with his head in his arms leaning against the window, was the son of a very rich land owner. A mark like any other, paid for in advance by an unidentifiable transaction through so many Routers anyone one following it would have toured the Earth. It was simple enough to surround his dreamstate with my own and plant the nexus I was given, one to incept the idea of murdering his father than proceeding to make an increasing amount of bad decisions culminating in the sale of his properties. The very long con.

I had just finished cleaning stray thoughts in his memory, brushing any hint of my involvement away, when I felt a sharp pain behind my eyes. All at once I was with him, floating in darkness looking at a lanky Chinese man dressed in a suit. And then I WAS him.

Wait, me?

Who?

Huh?

"Xi Jinping" I said to my inner self in clear Chinese, surprising even myself with the words and the sudden split apart of our bubbles.

"Who's there? How do you know my name?!" Xi exclaimed in my head.

"What the fuck is going on?" I wondered to myself .

"Beats me," Xi's voice whispered in my ear.

I looked around, everyone's bubble was recoiling away from mine. Xi's was still near the the front of the bus; he hadn't woken up. Then who the fuck is talking to me? There isn't a Virus strong enough to hold another Virus without them realizing it. I didn't feel like I was being read. I could usually tell when the Thought Police Viruses browsed through the citizens for their "safety."

"Welcome," Xi's voice echoed through me, resonating long after the words had been spoken, "to the DeepOuterNet."
